summary: Describes architectures for recording sessions in a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) environment. Recording is needed in places like call centers and financial trading, often for regulatory reasons, and is usually done by sending a copy of the media stream to a recording device.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7245 sets out how to record a call that uses SIP. One device, the recording client, listens in on the call and sends a copy of the audio to a recording server. The two of them hold their own separate SIP conversation, so the recording does not interfere with the call itself. The client also tells the people on the call that they are being recorded.

subtitle: How a phone call gets copied to a recorder: the pieces, the SIP conversation, and who must be told.

tldr.problem: Call centres and trading floors have to record every call for regulatory reasons, and the recorded audio has to be captured from the call without interrupting it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a recording client that keeps a copy of the media and sends it to a recording server over a second, separate SIP session. That session is set up with an ordinary SIP invitation and session description, and it can be paused and resumed by changing the direction attribute.
tldr.outcome: The document covers active recording only, where the client deliberately sends the copy. Passive capture from the network and lawful intercept are both out of scope, because in both cases the people on the call are not told.

sections.title: Recording a Call Without Breaking It
sections.content:
Session recording is a critical requirement in many communications environments such as call centres and financial trading. In some of these environments all calls must be recorded for regulatory, compliance and consumer protection reasons. Recording is typically performed by sending a copy of a media stream to a recording device. This document describes architectures for deploying session recording solutions as defined in the earlier document on use cases and requirements for SIP-based media recording.

The focus is on how sessions are established between the Session Recording Client and the Session Recording Server for the purpose of conveying the replicated media and the recording metadata, such as the identity of the parties involved, relating to the communication session. Once the server has received them they will typically be archived for retrieval at a later time; the procedures for archiving and retrieval are outside the scope of this document.

Only active recording is considered, where the client purposefully streams media to the server. Passive recording, where a recording device detects media directly from the network, for example using port mirroring, is out of scope, and so is lawful intercept, which takes account of the IETF policy on wiretapping.

The recording session uses the normal procedures for establishing an invitation-initiated SIP dialog, and the Session Description Protocol describes the media used during it. It is intended that some extensions to SIP, such as new headers and option tags, will be defined to support the requirements for media recording. The replicated media is required to be sent in real time to the server and is not buffered by the client, so that the server can analyse the media as it arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: Two conversations, not one. The call happens as normal, and a second, separate conversation carries a copy of the sound to the recorder. Nothing about the copy touches the call itself.

sections.title: The Parts and the Roles
sections.content:
A Session Recording Server is a SIP user agent that is a specialised media server or collector acting as the sink of the recorded media. It is typically a multi-port device able to receive media from several sources at once, and it is the sink of the recorded session metadata. A Session Recording Client is a SIP user agent that acts as the source of the recorded media, sending it to the server and providing metadata to it. The client is a logical function whose capabilities may be implemented across one or more physical devices: in practice it could be a personal device such as a SIP phone, a media gateway, a session border controller, or a media server integrated with an application server. The term is defined so that all of those can be addressed under one name.

The communication session is the session between two or more SIP user agents that is the subject of recording. The recording session is the SIP session between the client and the server, created for the purpose of recording that communication session. The replicated media is the copy of the media associated with the communication session, created by the client and sent to the server; it may contain all of the media, such as audio and video, or just a subset such as the audio alone, and it is part of the recording session. The recording metadata describes the communication session, for example the identities of the users taking part and the state of the dialog; it is typically archived with the replicated media and is delivered to the server in real time.

Two kinds of user agent matter. A recording-aware user agent knows about the SIP extensions associated with the communication session, so it can be told that the session is being recorded, and can say whether a recording should be started, paused, resumed or stopped. A recording-unaware user agent knows nothing of these extensions; it is still notified that a session is being recorded, and expresses its preferences by some other means that is out of scope for this architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: The recording client is the one that copies the call. The recording server is the one that stores it. The call itself is a third thing, separate from both.

sections.title: Where the Recording Client Can Live
sections.content:
Because the client is a logical function, it can sit in or be split between several kinds of device. A back-to-back user agent that has access to the media to be recorded may act as the client. It may already know that a session needs to be recorded before the communication session is established, or the decision may come afterwards. If the client decides to start the recording session it sends an invitation to the server; if the server decides, it sends an invitation to the client. That invitation carries information identifying the session as being established for recording, and prevents it being accidentally rerouted to a user agent that is not a server. The client is also responsible for telling the user agents in the call that the session is being recorded, and for honouring a request from a recording-aware user agent, or a configured policy, that the call should not be recorded.

A SIP endpoint may also act as the client, sending the replicated media to the server. Here too either the endpoint or the server can start the recording session with an invitation; the actual decision mechanism is out of scope.

A SIP proxy cannot act as the client, because a proxy has no access to the media and so has no way of enabling delivery of the copy to the server.

The client or the server may also be built in the media control architecture, in which an application server controls a media server. In that case the media server is the sink of the recording media and the application server is the sink of the metadata and the termination point for the signalling, when the server is built that way; and the other way round when the client is built that way.

In a conference, the conference focus and mixer may act as the client, and can supply media and metadata for each participant, including any side conversations that pass through the mixer. The focus can supply one mixed stream or separate streams per participant, and can also act as a recording-aware user agent when one of the participants is the client. Alternatively a participant's own endpoint can act as the client, in which case it has access to the media and metadata for that participant and may obtain further metadata from the focus, for instance through the conference event package.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything that can see the media can do the copying: a proxy in the middle of the call, a phone on the desk, or the equipment that mixes a conference. A pure signalling proxy sees no audio at all, so it cannot.

sections.title: Setting Up the Recording Session
sections.content:
Either the client or the server may start the recording session, and the recording session is independent of the communication session at both the dialog level and the session level. Media negotiation uses the ordinary SIP and session description capabilities, and existing transcoding and media encryption are not ruled out.

When the client starts it, it is provisioned with a URI for the server, resolved through the usual procedures, and it sends an invitation. The invitation includes an indication that the session is being established for recording, and for each media line a session description attribute of a=sendonly if the replicated media is to start immediately, or a=inactive if the client is not yet ready to transmit. The client then replicates the media streams that are to be recorded and sends them to the server. It may replicate all the media of the communication session or only a subset.

When the server starts it, the steps are mirrored: the server is provisioned with a URI for the client, sends an invitation with the same indication that the session is for recording, identifies the sessions that are to be recorded by a mechanism that depends on the client's policy, and includes a=recvonly for each media line if the session is to start immediately, or a=inactive if it is not yet ready to receive. If the server does not already know what media streams are available, it can make use of an offerless invitation, which lets the client make the first session description offer.

The server or the client can pause the recording by changing the direction attribute to a=inactive and resume it by changing it back to a=recvonly or a=sendonly. In a basic session with only audio, there are typically two audio streams between the two user agents, one in each direction, and they may be mixed at the client or not. If they are not mixed, two separate streams are sent to the server and the session description offer must describe two separate media streams; if they are mixed, a single mixed stream is sent.

The communication session and the recording session are negotiated separately, which may mean the client has to transcode between the two. If it cannot, it may limit the media formats it offers to the server according to what was negotiated on the call, or limit what it offers on the call if it already knows what the server supports; typically the server is the more capable device and may have a transcoder of its own. Finally, some environments impose a requirement known as lossless recording, and the RFC notes that a complete answer may involve several layers, from administering the network for appropriate quality of service, through reliable transmission of the recorded media, to protocol-level capabilities in the client and the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The recording conversation is set up like any other SIP call, with the twist that the direction attribute says who is sending. Setting it to inactive is how you pause the recording, and setting it back resumes it.

sections.title: Metadata, Notifications and Objections
sections.content:
The metadata model is defined in a companion document, and the metadata is carried from the client to the server using SIP-based mechanisms specified in another companion document. It is possible to transport metadata by non-SIP mechanisms, but that is out of scope, and it is possible to have a recording session with no metadata at all, in which case the server receives the metadata by some other means or not at all.

The users on the call are normally told that the call is being recorded, either by an announcement at the start of the session or by warning tones in the media. Because of the recording extensions, an indication that the call is being recorded can also be included in the SIP requests and responses associated with the communication session. The client provides that notification to all the user agents for which it is replicating received media, and when the client is acting as a SIP endpoint it also notifies the local user.

Finally, a recording-aware user agent may state its preference about whether the media should be recorded, either during the initial establishment of the session or during an established session. The mechanisms for that are specified in the companion protocol document.
sections.plainLanguage: Along with the audio, the recorder is told who was on the call, and the people on the call are told that the recording is happening. A user agent that understands the recording extensions can also object.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The recording session is a standard SIP dialog and media session, so it uses the existing SIP security mechanisms to protect both the recording session and the recording metadata. The intended use of the architecture is only for the case where users are aware that they are being recorded, and the architecture provides the means for the client to notify them. It is not intended to support lawful intercept, which in contrast requires that users are not informed.

Once the replicated media and the metadata have been received and archived, it is the server's responsibility to protect them. The stored content must be protected with a cipher at least as strong as the original content, although how the storage and retrieval are protected is out of scope. The keys used to store the data must be securely maintained by the server and released only to authorised parties, and how to secure those keys, authorise a receiving party and distribute the keying material is also out of scope.

The protection of the recording session should not be weaker than the protection of the call itself, and may need to be stronger because the media is retransmitted, which allows more opportunity for interception. This applies to both the signalling and the media paths. It is essential that the client authenticate the server, because the client must be certain that it is recording to the right recording system. It matters less that the server authenticate the client, but implementations must be able to perform mutual authentication. In some environments it is desirable not to decrypt and re-encrypt the media at all, meaning the same media encryption key is negotiated and used in both the call and the recording session; if the media are decrypted on the call and re-encrypted on the recording session, a new key must be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The recording is a copy of something private, so it needs the same protection as the original and then some, because a copy travels a second path where it can be intercepted. The recording server is responsible for keeping the stored recording safe once it has it.

viz.caption: THE CALL AND THE RECORDING ARE SEPARATE SESSIONS

left.title: Communication session
left.desc: The call itself, between the two parties. The recording is about this session.

right.title: Recording session
right.desc: A second SIP session between the recording client and the recording server, which carries the copy and the metadata.

viz.caption: WHERE THE RECORDING CLIENT CAN SIT

items.title: Back-to-back user agent
items.text: A proxy-like device in the middle of the call, which can see the media.

items.title: SIP endpoint
items.text: One of the phones on the call copies its own side of the conversation.

items.title: Conference focus
items.text: The equipment that mixes a conference can supply the mixed or per-participant streams.

items.title: Media control server
items.text: A media server steered by an application server can be the source or the sink.

items.title: Not a SIP proxy
items.text: A proxy has no access to the media, so it cannot deliver a copy.

messages.label: INVITE
messages.note: The client opens the recording session, marking it as being for recording, with a=sendonly or a=inactive.

messages.label: Notification
messages.note: The client tells the user agent on the call that the session is being recorded.

messages.label: RTP/RTCP
messages.note: A copy of the media is sent to the server in real time, without buffering.
